newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU delivers political compromise on EMU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: EU delivers political compromise on EMU budget pact.

text.p: A classic compromise, pitting the concerns of national sovereignty against economic expediency, underlined a European Union pact on Friday that seeks to curb budget deficits after monetary union.

After months of hard bargaining with its EU partners, Germany, the driving force behind the fiscal stability pact, secured a deal that aims to keep annual budget deficits below three percent of gross domestic product.
The blueprint of the plan, however, is several steps back from what Bonn had initially sought in its battle to ensure that the new euro single currency is as strong as its mark.
Uncertainty remains over how effective the pact will be in practice in disciplining the states which join the EU's planned economic and monetary union (EMU).

The financial markets reacted by selling the mark against the dollar, as well as against other European currencies viewed as having a chance of merging in the euro, due to be launched on January 1, 1999.
But at a political level, the fact the 15-nation bloc was able to agree to more restrictions on government borrowing is an achievement which some observers say merits considerable praise.
"I think to achieve a stability pact at all is a heroic effort," said economist Adrian Schmidt at Chase Manhattan Bank in London.

EU finance ministers said the pact balanced the conflicting concerns of EU states, particularly Germany and France who had differed sharply over the need for political involvement in the decision-making process.

"It is an attempt to balance sovereign rights and to recognise the need to avoid any ambiguity on exceptional and temporary (economic) circumstances," said Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn, president of the ministerial meeting.
Bonn had initially argued that the fines on governments running excessive should be unlimited. That battle was lost. EU ministers agreed a maximum ceiling for fines of 0.5 percent of total output.

Germany also wanted the entire procedure for fining states to be as automatic as possible. Here again, the ministers were able to wrestle control over determining whether a government would actually have to pay for its budgetary sins.

On perhaps the most contentious aspect of the so-called stability pact -- a strict definition of an economic downturn that would let a government avoid fines -- the resulting compromise was a range of growth, or box, that may be viewed as yet another escape hatch for fiscal offenders.

It would be an "exceptional and temporary" circumstance if GDP fell by 2.0 percent or more in the course of a year. But if growth slipped by 0.75 percent, a government would also have a chance to argue that this was an unusal event and might be let off the hook.
German officials, however, expressed satisfaction that they had secured a credible deal.

Juergen Stark, state secretary to the German finance ministry, told Reuters that under the terms of the agreement exemptions would only have been granted to EU nations in about 20 cases over the last 35 years.
What remains unclear, say experts, is whether there was any real chance for Germany to get all it wanted and even whether it thought it could.
As with most things in the EU, compromise is the order of the day, with governments often coming to the negotiating table with a set of demands which are known to be unacceptable.
"It's a typically good compromise because everybody will be able to say that they won," said Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt at a news conference.
The agreement now allows two other important elements of EMU to move forward on schedule.

These are a new Exchange Rate Mechanism, meant to link the euro to EU currencies left outside monetary union, and a legal framework which ensures the continued validity of financial contracts denominated in currencies which merge in the euro.
